examples.problem_statement:
Solve the system of equations using Cramer’s Rule:
\[ \left\{ \begin{array}{l} 3x - 2y - z - 4w = 7 \quad (1) \\ x + 3z + 2w = -10 \quad (2) \\ x + 4y + 2z + w = 0 \quad (3) \\ 2x + 3y + 3w = 1 \quad (4) \end{array} \right. \]

solution.operation: Set up the coefficient matrix D
solution.description: Read the four coefficients out of each equation in the fixed order x, y, z, w and stack them as the rows of the main determinant D. Equation (2) has no y term and equation (4) has no z term, so those places take a coefficient of 0.

Expand the four by four determinant along its first row, multiplying each first-row entry by its three by three minor and alternating the signs. The value is -210, and because it is not zero the system has a single solution that Cramer's Rule can produce.

solution.operation: Compute N_x by replacing first column with constants
solution.description: Build the numerator for x by copying D but writing the constants 7, -10, 0, 1 from the right-hand sides in place of the x column, then evaluate that determinant the same way to get -105.

solution.operation: Compute N_y by replacing second column with constants
solution.description: Do the same for y: the constant column now replaces the y coefficients while the other three columns stay exactly as they were in D, and the determinant evaluates to -315.

solution.operation: Compute N_z by replacing third column with constants
solution.description: Repeat once more for z, putting the constant column in the third position and leaving the rest of D untouched, which gives 525.

solution.operation: Compute N_w by replacing fourth column with constants
solution.description: Finally replace the fourth column, the w coefficients, with the constants and evaluate to get 315. All four numerators are now in hand.

solution.operation: Apply Cramer's Rule to find solutions
solution.description: Divide each numerator by the same denominator D to read off the unknowns. The common divisor -210 turns the four numerators into x = 1/2, y = 3/2, z = -5/2 and w = -3/2.
Substitute those four values back into equation (1). The left side collapses to 7, which matches the right side, so the solution checks out.

key_reminders: {'point': '[NOTE]: The above system permits some variation in procedure.'}
{'point': 'For example, having found x = 1/2 and y = 3/2 using determinants, the value of w may be obtained by substituting in (4) ...'}
{'point': 'and the value of z may then be obtained by substituting in (2) ...'}
{'point': 'The solution may be checked by substituting in (1) or (3).'}
common_mistakes: Skipping the zero coefficients: equation (2) has no y term and equation (4) has no z term, so those places in the determinant must be written as 0, not left out.
Losing the alternating plus and minus signs when expanding the four by four determinant along its first row.
Dividing the wrong way around: each unknown is its own numerator determinant divided by D, so x is -105 divided by -210, not -210 divided by -105.
repair_note: Rewrote all eight descriptions to narrate their own operation and result (which column is replaced, why D is computed first, how the four quotients are formed); replaced the auto-extracted QC_TRAP object in common_mistakes with three plain-string hazards specific to this system; visual_scaffold textual_scaffold -> equation_chain because the steps build a chain of determinant expressions ending in four divisions. technique_name Cramer's Rule is what the steps teach and was kept.

examples.problem_statement: (a) The system \left\{ \begin{array}{l} 3x - 2y = 1 \\ 4x + 3y = 41 \end{array} \right. has solution x = 5, y = 7.

solution.operation: Solve the subsystem of two equations for x and y.
solution.description: Take the pair of equations shown, 3x - 2y = 1 and 4x + 3y = 41, and solve them together; they pin down the single pair of values x = 5 and y = 7.

solution.operation: Substitute x = 5 and y = 7 into the third equation: 6x + 2y = 23.
solution.description: A system is consistent only if every one of its equations holds, so carry x = 5 and y = 7 into the equation held back, 6x + 2y = 23, and compare the two sides.

State the verdict from that test: if the substituted values make the last equation true, all the equations share one solution and the system is consistent; if the two sides disagree, no common solution exists.

examples.problem_statement: (b) The system \left\{ \begin{array}{l} 3x + y = 1 \\ 5x - 2y = 20 \end{array} \right. has solution x = 2, y = -5.

solution.operation: Solve the subsystem of two equations for x and y.
solution.description: Solve the displayed pair 3x + y = 1 and 5x - 2y = 20 together; the only values satisfying both at once are x = 2 and y = -5.

solution.operation: Substitute x = 2 and y = -5 into the third equation: 4x + 5y = -17.
solution.description: Test that pair in the equation held back, 4x + 5y = -17: the left side becomes 8 plus -25, which is -17, so this equation is satisfied too.
Because every equation is true for the same pair, the system is consistent and x = 2, y = -5 is its solution.

examples.answer: The given system is consistent with solution x = 2, y = -5.

examples.problem_statement: (c) The system \left\{ \begin{array}{l} x + y + z = 2 \\ 4x + 5y - 3z = -15 \\ 5x - 3y + 4z = 23 \end{array} \right. has solution x = 1, y = -2, z = 3.

solution.operation: Solve the subsystem of three equations for x, y, z.
solution.description: Solve the three displayed equations together; the triple that satisfies all of them at once is x = 1, y = -2, z = 3.

solution.operation: Substitute x = 1, y = -2, z = 3 into the fourth equation: 7x - y + 6z = 27.
solution.description: Substitute that triple into the remaining equation 7x - y + 6z = 27: the left side becomes 7 plus 2 plus 18, which is 27, so this equation holds as well.
Every equation of the system is satisfied by the same triple, so the system is consistent with solution x = 1, y = -2, z = 3.

examples.answer: The given system is consistent with solution x = 1, y = -2, z = 3.

examples.problem_statement: (d) The system \left\{ \begin{array}{l} x + y = 5 \\ y + z = 8 \\ x + z = 7 \end{array} \right. has solution x = 2, y = 3, z = 5.

solution.operation: Solve the subsystem of three equations for x, y, z.
solution.description: Solve the three displayed equations together; x = 2, y = 3, z = 5 is the only triple that satisfies all three.

solution.operation: Substitute x = 2, y = 3, z = 5 into the fourth equation: 5x - 5y + z = 1.
solution.description: Carry that triple into the remaining equation 5x - 5y + z = 1: the left side becomes 10 minus 15 plus 5, which is 0, not 1.
The one triple the first three equations allow fails the last equation, so no values satisfy the whole system and it is inconsistent.

key_reminders: {'point': '(NOTE: If the constant of the fourth equation of the system were changed from 1 to 0, the resulting system would be consistent.)'}
common_mistakes: Declaring the system consistent as soon as the displayed equations are solved, without testing those values in the equation that was held back.
Mishandling negative values during the substitution check, for example evaluating 5y at y = -5 as +25 instead of -25.

examples.problem_statement: Finding the Axis of Symmetry. In Fig. 22-5, find all axes of symmetry for the regular hexagon ABCDEF.

solution.operation: Understand the properties of a regular hexagon
solution.description: Start from what makes the hexagon regular: six equal sides and six equal angles. A regular polygon has as many axes of symmetry as it has sides, so expect six axes here and use that number as a check on the list built next.
Draw the three long diagonals joining opposite vertices, AD, BE and CF. Folding the hexagon along any one of them lays each half exactly onto the other, so all three are axes of symmetry.

solution.result: \text{Midpoints of opposite sides: } \frac{A+B}{2} \text{ and } \frac{D+E}{2}, \frac{B+C}{2} \text{ and } \frac{E+F}{2}, \frac{C+D}{2} \text{ and } \frac{F+A}{2}
solution.description: Now take the lines through the midpoints of opposite sides: midpoint of AB with midpoint of DE, BC with EF, and CD with FA. Each of these is perpendicular to the two sides it bisects and is also an axis of symmetry.
Add the two families found: three vertex-to-vertex diagonals plus three side-midpoint lines make six axes in all, matching the count predicted from the six sides in step 1.

solution.result: \text{Current answer mentions } AD, FC, BE, l, \text{ and two others}
solution.description: Compare that list against the axes labelled in the figure, which names AD, FC and BE along with a line l. The figure marks only part of the set, so the labelled axes alone do not account for all six.

solution.result: \text{Axes of symmetry: } AD, BE, CF, \text{ and lines through midpoints of } AB \text{ and } DE, BC \text{ and } EF, CD \text{ and } FA
solution.description: Write out the complete set: the diagonals AD, BE and CF, together with the lines through the midpoints of AB and DE, of BC and EF, and of CD and FA.

examples.answer: The regular hexagon has 6 axes of symmetry: three through opposite vertices (AD, BE, CF) and three through midpoints of opposite sides (through midpoints of AB and DE, BC and EF, CD and FA). In the figure, AD, FC, BE are the vertex-to-vertex axes; the line l is one of the side-midpoint axes (e.g., through midpoints of AB and DE); the other two side-midpoint axes are through midpoints of AF and CD, and BC and EF.

examples.problem_statement: Discovering Line Symmetry. Which of the objects in Fig. 22-6 exhibit line symmetry?

solution.description: Begin with the square: folding it down either midline or along either diagonal maps it onto itself, so it has line symmetry, with four axes.
Move to the isosceles right triangle: the altitude drawn to the hypotenuse folds one leg onto the other, so this figure has line symmetry along that single line.

Test the letter S: no vertical or horizontal fold maps it onto itself. Its balance comes from a half turn about its centre, which is point symmetry rather than line symmetry, so S is the object that fails the test.
Check the T-shape: a vertical fold down the stem carries the left arm onto the right arm, so the T-shape has line symmetry about that vertical line.

solution.operation: Examine object (e), a symmetric zigzag shape.
solution.description: Finish with the symmetric zigzag: its peaks and troughs mirror each other about a vertical line, so it has line symmetry too, leaving the letter S as the only object in the figure without any.

Assuming every diagonal of a polygon is an axis of symmetry; in a regular hexagon only the three joining opposite vertices are.
Calling the letter S symmetric because it looks balanced; its symmetry is a half turn about a point, not a fold along a line.

examples.problem_statement: Finding Images under a Reflection in a Point. Referring to Fig. 22-7, find $(a)$ $R_O(B)$, $(b)$ $R_O(C)$, $(c)$ $R_O(\overline{AD})$, $(d)$ $R_O(\angle AOB)$, and $(e)$ $R_O(ABCDEF)$.

solution.operation: Reflection of point B over point O
solution.description: A reflection in the point O carries each point straight through O to the point an equal distance beyond it. In this regular hexagon B and E sit opposite one another across O, so the image of B is E.

solution.operation: Reflection of point C over point O
solution.description: Apply the same half-turn idea to C: the vertex directly opposite C through the centre is F, so C maps to F.

solution.operation: Reflection of line segment AD over point O
solution.description: A and D are opposite vertices, so the segment AD runs through O itself. The reflection swaps its two endpoints, which leaves the segment as a whole exactly where it was.

solution.operation: Reflection of angle AOB over point O
solution.description: An angle maps to the angle formed by the images of its sides. Ray OA reflects to ray OD and ray OB reflects to ray OE, so angle AOB maps to angle DOE, congruent to the original.

solution.operation: Reflection of hexagon ABCDEF over point O
solution.description: Reflecting every vertex in O pairs A with D, B with E and C with F, so the six vertices are permuted among themselves and the hexagon lands back on itself: the figure has point symmetry about O.

examples.problem_statement: Finding Point Symmetry. Which of the following exhibit point symmetry? (a) Squares (b) Rhombuses (c) Scalene triangles (d) S

solution.description: Ask of each listed figure whether a half turn about some centre carries it onto itself. A square and a rhombus both do, turned about the intersection of their diagonals, and the letter S does about its own centre; a scalene triangle has no such centre. So every figure except (c) exhibits point symmetry.

key_reminders: {'point': 'Note: Use notation $R_O(P)$ to denote the image of point P under reflection in point O.'}
{'point': 'Remember: A figure exhibits point symmetry if it maps onto itself under a 180° rotation about a point.'}
{'point': 'Caution: Scalene triangles do not exhibit point symmetry because no point exists such that every point has an image directly opposite through that center.'}
common_mistakes: Expecting a point reflection to move every part of a figure: a segment through the centre, such as AD, maps onto itself.
Confusing point symmetry with line symmetry; the letter S has point symmetry but no axis of symmetry, while a scalene triangle has neither.

examples.problem_statement: In Fig. 22-15, find (a) The reflection of C in the y axis (b) The reflection of B in the origin. (c) The reflection of △CAB in the x axis

solution.description: Part (a) asks for the mirror image of C across the y axis. That mirror keeps a point at the same height and moves it to the other side, so the rule is that (x, y) becomes (-x, y).
Apply that rule to C(2,3): the x coordinate 2 changes sign to -2 while the y coordinate stays 3, giving the image (-2, 3).
Part (b) reflects B in the origin instead. That sends each point straight through the origin to the opposite side, so both coordinates change sign and (x, y) becomes (-x, -y).
Apply the origin rule to B(3,1): 3 becomes -3 and 1 becomes -1, so the image is (-3, -1).
Part (c) reflects the whole triangle in the x axis. This mirror keeps horizontal position and flips height, so the rule is that (x, y) becomes (x, -y).
Because a reflection carries a triangle to the triangle on the images of its vertices, apply the x axis rule to each one: C(2,3) goes to (2,-3), A(1,1) to (1,-1) and B(3,1) to (3,-1).
Join the three image points to name the result, triangle C'A'B' with C'(2,-3), A'(1,-1) and B'(3,-1). It is congruent to the original and sits below the x axis as its mirror image.

key_reminders: {'point': "In other words, m∠BAO = m∠B'A'O in Fig."}
{'point': '22-14(a), and that property appears to hold for other reflections.'}
{'point': 'As you will see, other properties are preserved as well.'}

{'point': 'Under a reflection in the x axis, the point (a, b) moves to (a, -b); under a reflection in the y axis, (a, b) moves to (-a, b); and under a reflection in the origin, (a, b) moves to (-a, -b).'}
{'point': 'These patterns hold only for these reflections.'}
common_mistakes: Negating the y coordinate for a reflection in the y axis; that mirror changes the sign of x and leaves y alone.
Changing both signs for a reflection in an axis: only the reflection in the origin sends B(3,1) to (-3,-1).

solution.description: Read the notation first: T with subscript (h, k) slides every point h units horizontally and k units vertically, so the rule is that (x, y) becomes (x + h, y + k).
Here the subscript is (-1, 1), so h is -1 and k is 1: this particular translation moves each point one unit left and one unit up.
Apply that shift to the first point, (1, 4), by adding the components coordinate by coordinate, which sets up 1 + (-1) and 4 + 1.
Carry out the two additions: 1 + (-1) is 0 and 4 + 1 is 5, so the image of (1, 4) is (0, 5).
The same translation acts on every point of the plane, so add the same pair (-1, 1) to the second point (-1, 2).
Complete the arithmetic: -1 + (-1) is -2 and 2 + 1 is 3, giving the image (-2, 3). Both points moved by the same shift, as a translation requires.

examples.problem_statement: Find the image of $\triangle ABC$ under the translation $T_{(1,2)}$, where $A = (0,0)$, $B = (1,1)$, and $C = (1,0)$.

solution.description: Translate the triangle one vertex at a time, starting with A(0,0): add the shift (1, 2) to it, forming 0 + 1 and 0 + 2.
Adding gives A' = (1, 2), the image of the first vertex.
Apply the same shift (1, 2) to the second vertex B(1,1), forming 1 + 1 and 1 + 2.
Adding gives B' = (2, 3), the image of the second vertex.
Now translate the last vertex C(1,0) with the same shift, forming 1 + 1 and 0 + 2.
Adding gives C' = (2, 2). Joining A', B' and C' produces the image triangle, the same size and shape as ABC but moved one unit right and two units up.

examples.answer: The image is $\triangle A'B'C'$ with vertices $A'(1,2)$, $B'(2,3)$, $C'(2,2)$

examples.problem_statement: Under a certain translation, $T(5,2) = (7,1)$. Find $T(-3,6)$ under the same translation.

solution.description: This time the shift is not given, only that the translation sends (5, 2) to (7, 1). Write that fact with unknown components h and k so they can be solved for.
Match the first coordinates: 5 + h has to equal 7, so h is 2, a shift of two units to the right.
Match the second coordinates: 2 + k has to equal 1, so k is -1, a shift of one unit down.
With the translation now known to be (2, -1), apply it to the new point (-3, 6) by adding the components as usual.
Finish the arithmetic: -3 + 2 is -1 and 6 + (-1) is 5, so the image of (-3, 6) under the same translation is (-1, 5).

key_reminders: {'point': 'As in a reflection, distance and angle measure are preserved in a translation.'}
{'point': '22-17 that (1, 4) and (-1, 2) are translated the same number of units in the same direction by the same translation T.'}
{'point': "All points are translated along ray AA' = OA', where A'(1,2) has the coordinates of the translation."}
common_mistakes: Shifting only one coordinate, or adding the horizontal component to y and the vertical component to x.
Recovering the translation vector backwards: from (5,2) going to (7,1) the components are image minus original, so h = 7 - 5 = 2 and k = 1 - 2 = -1.
Losing a sign when a component is negative, for example reading -1 + (-1) as 0 instead of -2.

examples.problem_statement: Finding the Rotation of a Point. Let A = (1,3) and B = (2,1), and find (a) Rot_{(O,90°)}(A), (b) Rot_{(O,90°)}(B), and (c) the image of AB under a rotation of 90° about O.

solution.operation: Recall rotation formula for 90° counterclockwise about origin
solution.description: Fix the rule before touching any point: a quarter turn counterclockwise about the origin carries (a, b) to (-b, a), so the old height becomes the new horizontal position, with its sign reversed.
Apply that rule to A(1,3). The y coordinate 3 becomes the new x with its sign changed, and the old x, 1, becomes the new y, so the image is A' = (-3, 1).
Rotate B(2,1) by the same rule: its y coordinate 1 changes sign to give the new x, and its x coordinate 2 becomes the new y, so B' = (-1, 2).

solution.operation: Determine the image of segment AB
solution.result: Segment AB rotates to segment A'B' where A' = (-3,1) and B' = (-1,2)
solution.description: A rotation carries a segment to the segment joining the images of its endpoints, so segment AB rotates to the segment from A'(-3,1) to B'(-1,2). Rotating the two endpoints was therefore enough to answer part (c).

Check the work with a length: AB measures the square root of 5, and the distance from A' to B' comes out to the square root of 5 as well. A rotation is a rigid motion, so this agreement confirms both image points were placed correctly.

examples.answer: (a) (-3,1); (b) (-1,2); (c) Image is segment from A'(-3,1) to B'(-1,2)
